newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Netanyahu beset by world criticism, rebel hawks.
newsitem.headline: Netanyahu beset by world criticism, rebel hawks.

text.p: Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, buffeted by crosswinds of condemnation over plans for a West Bank troop pullout and a new Jewish settlement, is battling to stave off rebellion in his ruling coalition.
The U.N. Security Council was due to meet late on Friday to vote on a resolution calling on Israel to rescind its February decision to build a Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem.

Palestinians accused Israel of killing the peace process by approving on Friday plans to hand over an additional fraction of the West Bank. The scope of the pullout -- decreed by Israel without negotiation with the Palestinians -- was denounced by the PLO as insufficient and in violation of peace accords.
Israeli hawks, accusing Netanyahu of overstepping his bounds in surrendering parts of the biblical Land of Israel, threatened to bolt the ruling coalition.
Netanyahu countered with a scarcely veiled threat to seek other, more moderate partners if his government were shaken.
"I hope they won't force us to consider the possibility of a unity government," Netanyahu told Israel Channel One Television, referring to a possible coalition with the centre-left Labour.
Speaking to Israel's Channel Two Television Netanyahu defended the pullout as a balance "between guarding our assets and progress in a process which is crucial for our future".
Under the cabinet decision two percent of the West Bank -- land now under full Israeli control -- would be handed over along with seven percent now under joint Israel-PLO rule.
Israel already handed three percent of the West Bank to the PLO under a 1993 peace deal, including eight major Arab towns.
Israeli media said the pullout was likely to begin by the middle of next week.

In a news conference, Netanyahu said of rightist opponents, "Maybe there are people who want to blow up the (peace) process". But he said he had stood up to Palestinians and Israeli doves who pressed for pulling out of 30 percent of the West Bank.
Israel's key ally Washington has endorsed the Israeli proposal. Palestinians vehemently oppose it.
"What the Israeli government has done with its decision is kill this (peace) process," said senior PLO official Ahmed Korei, who negotiated the broad 1993 peace deal with Israel.
Asked by Israel Radio if he backed halting the talks, Korei said "Without any doubt."

The PLO was already enraged at Israel's decision last month to build a new settlement of 6,500 homes in East Jerusalem, viewing it as an attempt to pre-empt talks on the future of what Palestinians see as the capital of a future state.

Egyptian Foreign Minister Amr Moussa, speaking in Washington on the eve of a visit by President Hosni Mubarak, said Israeli actions had "gravely affected" the credibility of the peace process in the region.
The United States opposed the settlement plan.

As rank and file Likud members demonstrated against Netanyahu on Friday at a busy Tel Aviv intersection, Deputy Education Minister Moshe Peled of the hawkish Tsomet party said he would resign over the handover of more land to the PLO.

Later in the month Netanyahu faces a no-confidence vote. Eight of the 66 members of the ruling coalition have hinted they may bolt. A no-confidence vote requires a 61-vote majority in the 120-seat parliament in order to bring down the government.
Analysts said the hardliners' public opposition increased the likelihood Netanyahu might opt for a "unity" government.
"The sharpest opposition to the prime minister is coming from his own camp," said political commentator Yaron Dekel.
"The (withdrawal) decision nearly failed to pass, and the government in its present makeup will find it very difficult to function politically for an extended period."
